NOVELTY STATEMENT
The standard practice for preventing ice-credit-loss in district cooling storage banks relies on **tank imaging or direct level measurement** combined with a fixed energy-balance inventory model that assumes constant volumetric efficiency; this delivers a MONITORING/INDICATION scheme where the threshold is a static "minimum ice mass" alarm.
My mechanism delivers the same MONITORING/INDICATION class but departs by using a **dynamic hydraulic-thermal coupling ratio** derived from existing pump current and glycol temperature differentials to infer the *effective heat transfer surface area* available for ice formation/melting, rather than relying on a static volume-to-energy assumption; the failure-physics connection is that ice-credit loss occurs when the effective surface area for heat exchange degrades (due to slurry packing or thermal stratification) faster than the inventory estimate compensates, causing a divergence between *theoretical* ice formation rate (based on glycol delta-T) and *actual* energy absorption rate (inferred from pump work and thermal sink stability).

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing relation is the Second Law constraint on heat transfer rate $\dot{Q} = U A \Delta T_{lm}$. In a glycol loop charging ice, $\dot{Q}$ is limited by the plate HX capacity. The pump current $I_p$ correlates to flow rate $Q_v$ via the pump affinity laws ($Q_v \propto \omega \propto I_p$ for constant V/Hz drive or $Q_v \propto I_p^{1/2}$ for VFD). The thermal power delivered is $\dot{Q}_{glycol} = m c_p \Delta T_{glycol}$. If the system is charging ice effectively, $\dot{Q}_{glycol} \approx \dot{Q}_{ice\_formation}$. If ice-credit loss is imminent (i.e., the "ice" isn't actually forming or is not usable), the effective $UA$ drops, or the thermal sink temperature rises, causing $\Delta T_{glycol}$ to widen or the pump to draw higher current for the same thermal load due to increased viscosity/friction if the loop is not properly mixed.
Magnitude verification: For a 40 MWh bank, typical charging power is ~5 MW. With glycol supply/return delta-T of 2.5 K, mass flow $m = \frac{5 \times 10^6}{3000 \times 2.5} \approx 667 \, \text{kg/s}$ (~2400 m³/h). A 5% loss in effective $UA$ (ice-credit erosion) would require a 5% increase in flow (current) or a 5% increase in $\Delta T$ to maintain the same MW, detectable within sensor noise of <1% if baseline is known.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
(a) Data Ingestion Module: Ingest existing **glycol supply/return temperatures** (stated sensor) and **loop pump current** (stated telemetry) via existing SCADA gateway; no new hardware installed.
(a) Baseline Model Calculator: Compute nominal specific heat capacity $c_p$ and mass flow correlation $f(I_p)$ from **stated nameplate data** of the pump and glycol concentration; tag DERIVED.
(b) Dynamic Ratio Logic: Implement a firmware block that calculates the **Hydraulic-Thermal Efficiency Index (HTEI)**: $HTEI = \frac{\Delta T_{supply-return}}{I_{pump}}$ during charge hours; tag CALCULATED from already-recorded signals.
(b) Threshold Generator: Derive the HTEI threshold from **stated physical relation**: The minimum expected HTEI corresponds to the maximum flow required to maintain plate HX design $\Delta T$ at 100% ice formation rate; tag DERIVED from stated specs.
(c) Alarm Condition: Trigger "Ice-Credit-Loss" predictor if HTEI deviates >2% from the derived theoretical curve for >15 minutes during charge; tag ALREADY-RECORDED input stream.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
Installability: No tank imaging, no new sensors; uses existing SCADA tags, so burden is ZERO incremental hardware. Operability: Logic runs in existing PLC/controller, no operator training required beyond standard alarm review. Maintenance: No calibration drift from new sensors; relies on existing temperature/current calibration which is standard. Cost Class: Same as standard software alarm updates, significantly lower than installing ultrasonic/level gauges (standard practice). Heavier logic complexity is worth it because it avoids the high cost and false-positive rates of tank imaging in slurry environments.
EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Retrieve 30 days of historical **glycol temperatures** and **pump current** from existing logs. Pass/Fail: Compute HTEI for each hour. Identify hours where **inventory estimate** (stated input) showed no ice formation despite positive net heat removal. In those "bad" hours, HTEI must be outside the 95% confidence band of the "good" charging hours. Kill Criterion: If the HTEI distribution for "bad" and "good" hours overlaps >50%, the mechanism fails to predict and is rejected. Duration: 4 hours computational analysis. Validation Source: Uses **already-recorded** logs and **stated** inventory estimates; no new data collection.

CONSTRAINT BIND
The primary stated indicator is **inventory estimate from charge hours**; my predictor supplements this by detecting the *process* anomaly (HTEI deviation) that causes the inventory to become invalid *before* the peak-day check. The pump current and temperatures are secondary inputs used only to infer the physical validity of the inventory calculation. No new instrumentation is used, strictly adhering to the user constraint of "no tank imaging" and "no new instrumentation."
